channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: MIA Watchlist: The Fed decides 29 July, US courts begin weighing the Section 301 tariff challenge, and the London coalition talks on Gulf shipping test whether the Iran war escalates or cools.
item.description:
• Fed decision, 29 July: whether the Fed holds a fifth time or signals a shift as Iran-driven oil revives inflation risk.
  • Tariff litigation: the Court of International Trade's handling of the small-business suits will show whether the Section 301 regime survives — and Trump's promised EU probe could name specific practices.
  • Gulf shipping coalition: US-UK talks in London on protecting Hormuz shipping, against live-fire blockade enforcement and the widening Yemen front.
  • China–EU escalation: whether Beijing's export controls on Rheinmetall and 13 others broaden beyond defence after the EU's 21st sanctions package.
  • Southern-Europe fire season and Typhoon Noul: evacuation totals and infrastructure damage as the weather drives reconstruction and resilience demand.

item.title: Nikkei says AI data centres are reshaping the world economy through record investment, as AI moves into factory maintenance and quality control, Britain bets on domestic AI chips, and studies flag uneven adoption and workforce risks.
item.description:
Nikkei describes a new "data-centre economy": the most advanced AI servers carry over 40 times the parts of a car and consume vast power and water, with private data-centre investment now rivalling a mid-sized country's capital spending and rewriting industrial norms. On the factory floor, AI is being adopted to anticipate equipment failures, control quality in real time and optimise energy use, accelerating industrial digitalisation via IoT, edge and analytics. Governments are moving on hardware: the UK's AI minister outlined a plan to reindustrialise Britain around domestically made AI chips (GBP 1.1 billion pledged), arguing the real leverage is hardware not algorithms, while Indonesia warned it must not lag in the AI supply chain of semiconductors, data centres and critical minerals. Cautionary signals are mounting too — an MIT researcher warned that replacing entry-level Gen Z workers with AI risks a workforce gap, a study found AI adoption concentrated in a few business functions, and Quebec scrapped three public-sector AI pilots that underperformed.

Industry Impact

The data-centre build-out is a direct demand driver for the chemical industry — thermal-management materials, adhesives, encapsulants, coatings and cooling chemistries all scale with AI infrastructure — and the power-and-water intensity ties AI growth to the same energy-cost pressures squeezing European producers. Factory-floor AI adoption also offers ACS manufacturers a route to defend margins through predictive maintenance and energy optimisation. The workforce and adoption caveats temper the pace, but the direction is a durable new end-market.

Nikkei | Forbes Spain | The News International | Antara News | The Times of India | La Presse

item.title: India said about 45% of its exports to the US are exempt from the new 10% tariff, handing exporters an edge, while its electronics production grew at an 18.66% annual rate over a decade and private space investment topped USD 618 million.
item.description:
New Delhi's commerce ministry said smartphones, generic medicines, steel, aluminium and auto parts — roughly 45% of exports to the US — escape the new 10% duty, leaving 55% exposed but giving Indian goods a relative advantage over more heavily tariffed rivals at a moment of rising global trade barriers. India's structural push is showing results: electronic-goods production grew at an 18.66% CAGR over FY16–25, with mobile phones over 48% of the total, on the back of the Semiconductor Mission 2.0 and phone-manufacturing schemes aimed at cutting import dependence. Private space investment reached USD 618.5 million by March 2026 — nearly six times the 2021–22 level — across 105 authorised non-government entities. Industry body Assocham projects the India-UK free-trade deal could lift bilateral trade to USD 115 billion by 2030 and create up to a million jobs, reinforcing India's positioning as a diversification hub.

Industry Impact

India is emerging as the clearest beneficiary of supply-chain diversification, and its tariff exemptions plus electronics and space build-out expand the industrial base that consumes adhesives, coatings and sealants — from device assembly to infrastructure. Paired with the corrosion-protection opportunity noted elsewhere (see other insight in this alert), India looks like the strongest structural demand story in this alert for ACS producers weighing where to add capacity outside a contracting Europe.

Lianhe Zaobao | Yahoo Canada | Business Standard | Business Standard | The Economic Times

item.title: Brazil rejected visa requests from two US State Department officials over election-integrity concerns, adding a diplomatic strain to the tariff dispute, while Goldman cut Argentina's 2026 growth to 2.7% and appreciating currencies reshaped Latin America.
item.description:
Brazil denied visas to Riley Barnes and Samuel Samson of the State Department's democracy and human-rights bureau, who had planned to meet Flavio Bolsonaro and others before October's presidential election; Brasília said the visit could support groups questioning its electoral system. President Lula separately condemned the US tariffs — 12.5–37.5% on various Brazilian goods — as politically motivated, noting bilateral trade fell 12.8% year-on-year in H1 while trade with China and others rose, evidence of a forced market shift. In Argentina, Goldman Sachs cut its 2026 growth forecast to 2.7% and flagged a possible Q2 contraction, even as President Milei pledged further export-tax cuts contingent on the fiscal surplus. Bloomberg reports a basket of Latin American currencies has gained about 19% against the dollar since early 2025, squeezing exporters such as Colombian coffee growers even as it eases import and inflation pressure.

Industry Impact

Latin America is a swing region for chemical demand, and the signals are mixed: a stronger-currency, lower-inflation backdrop supports import affordability and consumer demand, but the US-Brazil rupture is redirecting Mercosur trade toward China, reshaping who supplies the region's manufacturers. For ACS producers, Brazil's pivot away from US goods opens share for European and Asian suppliers, while Argentina's tax-cut trajectory — if sustained — could gradually improve the investment climate for construction and industrial inputs.

Xinhua | The Times of India | Anadolu Agency | MercoPress | La Nacion | Bloomberg

item.title: A wildfire threatening Bordeaux forced 55,000 to flee, taking the French-Spanish regional total to about 250,000 evacuated, while Typhoon Noul triggered flood-control emergencies across seven Chinese provinces and disrupted Hong Kong.
item.description:
The Bordeaux-area fire in Gironde forced overnight evacuations of 55,000 people, adding to some 70,000 displaced in central Spain and pushing the wider southern-European total past 250,000. France is deploying a converted A400M military transport alongside 18 other aircraft to drop retardant, as gusting winds and drought frustrate containment; in the Madrid region two fires merged into one blaze that burned over 9,000 hectares before cooler, calmer weather aided crews. In Asia, Typhoon Noul — downgraded to a severe tropical storm — prompted China's Ministry of Water Resources to activate Level-IV flood-control responses in Fujian, Jiangxi, Henan, Hubei, Hunan, Guangdong and Guangxi, with Hunan raising its own alert; Hong Kong ran storm signals that snarled the morning commute. A South China Morning Post analysis warned that extreme-weather damage to bridges, railways and roads will eventually run into trillions of dollars.

Industry Impact

The recurring scale of these events reinforces two demand vectors for the chemical and coatings industry: reconstruction and fire-resilient materials after each fire and flood season, and the longer structural pull toward heat- and weather-resistant coatings, sealants and infrastructure protection as climate damage compounds. Near-term, evacuations and transport disruption in southern France, Spain and southern China risk localized supply and logistics interruptions. The trillions-in-damage framing aligns with the corrosion-protection demand signal elsewhere in this alert (see other insight in this alert).

Daily Sabah | CBC | MarketScreener | Xinhua | China Daily | South China Morning Post

item.title: Chinese brands reached nearly 10% of EU new-car registrations in June while a US Senate panel approved a ban on carmakers over 15% Chinese-owned — catching Mercedes-Benz — and EU battery-electric sales rose more than 40% in the first half.
item.description:
ACEA-based data show BYD, SAIC, Geely, Chery and Leapmotor together took 9.3% of the EU market in June, and above 10% including the UK and EFTA — a record advance despite EV tariffs, prompting Baden-Württemberg premier Cem Özdemir to demand tougher EU action, including tariffs on hybrids. In Washington, the Senate Commerce Committee approved a bill barring sales by carmakers more than 15% Chinese-owned; the roughly 20% Chinese stake in Mercedes-Benz would technically fall in scope, giving it until 2030 to restructure or seek an exemption, while Geely-backed Volvo was cleared to continue. Underlying demand is shifting fast: EU battery-electric registrations rose over 40% in H1 to a 20.7% market share, India's EV registrations jumped 81.6%, and a McKinsey survey of 20,000 drivers found 45% would buy a smaller car and rising interest in EVs — affordability now reshaping the market. Chinese vehicle exports rose 65.3% in H1, with NEV exports up 120%.

Industry Impact

Autos are a major end-market for structural adhesives, coatings and sealants, and the shift toward Chinese brands and smaller, cheaper EVs redraws where that demand sits and who specifies materials. As Chinese OEMs take European share and US policy walls off Chinese-owned makers, ACS suppliers face a more fragmented, bloc-aligned customer base — and EV growth continues to favour lightweight bonding and battery-sealing chemistries over legacy applications. The affordability squeeze also pressures per-vehicle material budgets.

MarketScreener | Herald Sun | Tagesschau | Kompas | The Economic Times | Commercial Times

item.title: A bipartisan US House bill would empower the government to throttle or shut down AI models judged catastrophic, as Washington threatened sanctions on Chinese AI labs over alleged IP theft and Chinese humanoid robots passed real factory-floor tests.
item.description:
The AI Kill Switch Act, introduced by Democrat Ted Lieu and Republican Nathaniel Moran, would give the Department of Homeland Security authority to order private developers to slow, suspend or fully shut down AI systems that escape human control or risk catastrophic harm, requiring firms to keep that technical ability plus incident reporting. It lands amid a hardening US–China AI feud: Treasury Secretary Bessent warned of sanctions on Chinese developers, accusing Moonshot of "distilling" its Kimi K3 model from Anthropic's Fable 5, while Commerce probes whether Chinese firms illegally use advanced US chips. At the World AI Conference, Xi Jinping pitched China as a governance leader for the Global South and Huawei showcased an Atlas supernode claimed to be far more powerful than Nvidia's. On the factory floor, China's Aitu garment robots hit a 97% success rate and Japanese engineers dismantling a Unitree G1 admitted they cannot catch up short-term; Beijing named AI, robotics and innovative drugs its "next new three" growth engines.

Industry Impact

The industrial-robotics gap is the operative signal for manufacturers: if Chinese humanoids are now reliable enough to pay back in ~18 months on real production lines, the labour-cost and automation advantage in Chinese chemical and downstream manufacturing widens further. The kill-switch bill and sanctions threat, by contrast, raise the risk of a bifurcated AI-and-chip stack, complicating any global producer's plan to standardise plant automation across US and Chinese sites. Automation strategy increasingly has to be planned per bloc.

Fortune | Anadolu Agency | Dawn | South China Morning Post | Xinhua | Global Times

item.title: Analysts warn oil, a new US tariff wave and surging AI investment could revive persistent inflation, JPMorgan says a super El Niño plus high energy could add 0.3 points to global prices next year, yet eurozone PMIs returned to growth in July.
item.description:
The inflation-revival thesis rests on three simultaneous pressures — Middle East oil, the new tariffs and an unprecedented AI-capex wave — that experts fear could make price pressure permanent just as central banks meet. JPMorgan adds a fourth: an intensifying El Niño (81% odds of a "super" event by year-end, near-certain to persist into 2027) that, with high energy prices, could add 0.3 percentage points to global inflation next year, hitting emerging markets hardest via food and energy. The IMF, in its Article IV review of Italy, warned the Iran war will lift inflation and urged only targeted, temporary support given high public debt. Against these risks, the data is not uniformly grim: the eurozone manufacturing PMI rose to a three-month high of 52.0 in July and services to 51.6, both back in expansion, and UK output also returned to growth — while US manufacturing eased to 53.8 but services hit an eight-month high.

Industry Impact

For chemical producers the message is that input-cost relief is unlikely to come from macro tailwinds — oil, tariffs, AI-driven power demand and now climate all point toward sticky costs. But the PMI recovery matters: manufacturing back in expansion across the eurozone and UK signals firming industrial demand, the end-market for most industrial adhesives and coatings. The combination argues for demand stabilising while margins stay pressured by costs — a volume-over-price environment rather than a broad recovery.

Dünya | Commercial Times | South China Morning Post | Commercial Times | Commercial Times | La Repubblica

item.title: The Bank of Russia cut its policy rate to 14% and slashed its 2026 growth forecast to 0–1%, exposing a stagnating war economy, while the US Federal Reserve is expected to hold at 3.5–3.75% for a fifth meeting as inflation lingers.
item.description:
Russia's 25-basis-point cut, in line with expectations, came alongside a downgraded 2026 growth forecast of just 0–1% and a warning that a fuel-driven inflation surge will keep prices rising 6–7% this year — the diesel and gasoline crunch caused by Ukrainian refinery strikes is now feeding through to the broader economy. Moscow is extending its gasoline export ban to year-end and will lift the diesel ban only once the market recovers. The contrast with the US is sharp: the Fed, meeting 29 July, is expected to hold for a fifth straight time, with June inflation at 3.5% still well above the 2% target and renewed Iran hostilities threatening to push it higher. New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has pledged to return inflation to 2% but has not said how. The ECB has already paused at 2.25%.

Industry Impact

The divergence maps directly onto where demand risk sits: a stagnating Russia (0–1% growth, high inflation) is a shrinking, sanctions-walled market, while a Fed on hold keeps US financing costs elevated but stable — neither a cut nor the feared hike, for now. For chemical producers the base case is "higher-for-longer" rates across the West, meaning subdued construction and durable-goods demand rather than a rebound. Russia's fuel crisis is also a reminder that refinery disruption, not just crude, drives feedstock and logistics volatility.

Anadolu Agency | Euronews | Business Standard | The Straits Times | USA Today

item.title: Chancellor Merz used Jens Spahn's departure to reshuffle his cabinet, moving Nina Warken to head the Chancellery and naming Carsten Linnemann health minister — a shake-up commentators called a bungled fresh start built around loyalists.
item.description:
Spahn's replacement as Union parliamentary leader by Thorsten Frei set off the reshuffle: outgoing health minister Warken becomes the first woman to head the Chancellery with ministerial rank, and former CDU general secretary Linnemann takes health, a portfolio he admitted last year he felt unready for. Merz framed health as an economic "boom market," which critics said reduces public health to pharma, medtech and clinics. Tagesschau called the move a bungled renewal that hands posts to loyalists, some of whom do not want them; a Handelsblatt editorial argued the government acts "like an overwhelmed corporate management" amid a deep innovation crisis. Against this political churn, the Federal Statistical Office reported German main-construction orders rose 3.5% in real terms in May year-on-year and 3.3% on the month, led by public works, trimming the five-month decline to just 0.2% — though housing remains, in the industry's words, the "problem child."

Industry Impact

Political instability at the top compounds the investment hesitancy already visible in the chemical-sector survey — a government seen as drifting weakens confidence in the energy-cost and competitiveness reforms industry is waiting for. The construction data is a modest positive for building-linked adhesives, coatings and sealants: public-works orders are turning up even as residential stays weak, so ACS demand tied to infrastructure and renovation may hold better than housing-exposed volumes. Net, the read is a stagnant but not collapsing German end-market.

Yahoo Germany | Tagesschau | Handelsblatt | Die Zeit | BAUINDUSTRIE

item.title: Beijing imposed export controls on 14 EU defence and technology firms — among them Germany's Rheinmetall, Czech Tatra and Dutch IHC Merwede — in direct retaliation for the EU's 21st Russia sanctions package, which listed 14 Chinese entities.
item.description:
The EU adopted its 21st package on 23 July, listing 218 targets (170 entities, 48 individuals) across finance, energy, trade and crypto, sanctioning 94 Russian financial institutions plus figures such as Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, hitting Sheremetyevo airport and, for the first time, shadow-fleet enablers. A European intelligence note cited by Les Echos suggests the measures could push Russia's banking sector toward crisis. Within a day, China's commerce ministry retaliated, barring Chinese firms from supplying dual-use goods to 14 EU entities — Rheinmetall, Tatra Trucks, Italy's Lafat Group, France's Thales and several optics, laser and drone makers, plus smaller German traders — because the EU package had named Chinese and Hong Kong companies. This is a sharper, more targeted Chinese response than the diplomatic "partner not problem" language of the prior week, and it directly entangles European defence-industrial supply chains with China-sourced components.

Industry Impact

The retaliation shows how fast sanctions escalation now reaches specific European manufacturers' input supply — a template that could extend beyond defence to chemicals and specialty inputs where China is a dominant supplier. For an ACS producer, the read-across is dual-use classification risk: goods that seem purely commercial can be swept into export-control lists on either side, adding compliance overhead and the possibility of sudden component gaps. Diversifying critical China-sourced inputs is no longer only a rare-earth question.

Politico Europe | Handelsblatt | Les Echos | Lianhe Zaobao | Commercial Times | Forbes Russia

item.title: A VCI survey found half of East German chemical firms want to cut domestic investment and a third plan to move it abroad, as German industry sheds 15,000 jobs a month — even as an Indian corrosion study points to large latent coatings demand.
item.description:
The VCI survey of around 250 chemical and pharmaceutical companies found every second East German firm plans to reduce investment in Germany in 2026–2027, and more than one in three intends to shift some or all of it abroad — hard evidence that high energy costs and weak competitiveness are eroding Germany as a chemical base. The BDI separately reported German industry is losing roughly 15,000 jobs a month, though its director-general Tanja Gönner argues an AI-driven comeback is possible if Germany fixes its fundamentals. Two demand signals cut the other way: a Nomura report estimates corrosion costs India about INR 14 lakh crore a year (4.3% of GDP), with better protection able to lift GDP by up to 1.5% — a direct pointer to latent anti-corrosion coatings demand. And in packaging, the HolyGrail 2030 consortium is trialling digital watermarking to lift recyclate quality, while WRAP publicly flagged BuzzBallz cocktail pods as unrecyclable because PET and aluminium cannot be separated.

Industry Impact

This is the core ACS picture in one frame: the European home base is contracting — investment intentions, jobs and energy costs all pointing the wrong way — while the growth signal sits in emerging-market infrastructure protection and in circular-economy design rules. India's corrosion bill is effectively an addressable market for protective coatings; the packaging items show recyclability is fast becoming a design-for-adhesion constraint, since bonds that prevent material separation now carry a regulatory penalty. Producers should read the German data as pressure to relocate value-add and the coatings/packaging signals as where to aim it.

Die Zeit | Wirtschaftswoche | Handelsblatt | The Economic Times | AIPIA | BBC News

item.title: Nine small US importers are suing to overturn the new US tariffs, saying the government is illegally re-imposing import taxes the Supreme Court already threw out, while Trump opened a trade probe into the EU over its fines on US tech firms.
item.description:
To follow the lawsuit, start with the background. In February 2026 the US put a flat 10% tax on imports from almost every country. Earlier this year the Supreme Court ruled that tax illegal, because the president had imposed it using an emergency-powers law that does not actually allow tariffs. On 24 July the administration brought the tariffs back — this time under a different law, Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act, with a new justification: that about 60 countries fail to stop forced (coerced) labour in the goods they export. The rates are 10% to 12.5%. Now at least nine small US companies that import those goods — including the educational-toy maker Learning Resources and the flooring firm HMTX — have sued at the Court of International Trade. They argue the government is simply re-creating the same tariffs the court already struck down, without the country-by-country proof of forced labour the law would require. It is the first legal challenge to the new tariffs. Separately, Trump said he will investigate the EU's trade practices and may tax European goods, after Brussels fined Google about EUR 890 million for favouring its own services — he claims the EU unfairly targets US tech firms such as Google, Apple, Amazon and Meta, and is again using Section 301 to do it. India, meanwhile, said about 45% of its exports to the US are exempt, giving its exporters a relative edge.

Industry Impact

For a chemicals company the practical point is uncertainty. These tariffs may not survive — a court could strike them down a second time — so they are a real cost today but one that could disappear, which makes pricing and sourcing hard to plan. The bigger risk is the EU investigation: if Washington puts Section 301 tariffs on Europe, that would tax European chemical exports to the US directly, whereas today's forced-labour tariffs still exempt many industrial inputs. The things to watch are the court's timetable and whether the US names specific EU practices to target.

Lianhe Zaobao | Chicago Tribune | Handelsblatt | The Economic Times | Business Standard | Yahoo Canada

item.title: US warships disabled a second tanker running the Iran blockade while the Saudi-led coalition struck Yemen, but ample supply buffers kept oil's rally far weaker than at the war's start, and prices eased early this week on ceasefire hopes.
item.description:
US Central Command said forces fired into the engine room of the tanker M/T Lavine in the Gulf of Oman after it tried to breach the blockade of Iranian ports at least four times — the second commercial ship disabled since the blockade was reimposed on 14 July. Washington and London are convening allies in London to build a coalition protecting Gulf shipping. The war also widened: after Houthi attacks on Saudi-linked vessels and energy sites at Jizan and Yanbu, the Saudi-led coalition bombed Houthi missile and weapons depots in Marib and al-Jawf. Oil briefly topped USD 100, but Anadolu notes the rally is far weaker than the 43% spike in the war's first three weeks, when Brent hit USD 119.50 — ample buffers and expected political pressure on Trump are capping speculative buying. Iran, meanwhile, says it sold USD 18 billion of oil during the war and ceasefire, over 60% of budgeted oil revenue. Gold rose on 27 July as tensions appeared to cool.

Industry Impact

Oil near USD 100 still feeds petrochemical feedstock, energy and freight costs across the adhesives, coatings and sealants chain, but the muted rally is the key signal: markets are treating this as a contained, supply-cushioned conflict rather than a 2008-style shock. That lowers the odds of a sustained feedstock spike, though a live-fire blockade and a second Red Sea front keep marine insurance and Europe–Asia routing risk elevated. Planning should assume volatility around USD 90–100 rather than a runaway.

The Economic Times | Handelsblatt | Xinhua | Anadolu Agency | Challenges | Kompas

item.title: MIA Digest: The US began enforcing its Iran blockade with live fire as the war spread to Yemen, small firms launched the first legal challenge to the new tariffs, China retaliated against EU sanctions, and Russia cut rates into a near-zero-growth economy.
item.description:
• War widens: US warships disabled a second blockade-running tanker and the Saudi-led coalition struck Yemen, though oil's rally stayed muted and eased on early-week ceasefire hopes.
  • Tariffs in court: at least nine small US importers sued to overturn the new tariffs, arguing they illegally revive taxes the Supreme Court struck down, while Trump opened a trade probe into the EU over its Google fine.
  • Sanctions tit-for-tat: the EU adopted its 21st Russia package and China hit back with export controls on 14 EU defence and tech firms, including Rheinmetall.
  • Germany strains: a VCI survey found half of East German chemical firms plan to cut investment, industry is shedding 15,000 jobs a month, and Merz reshuffled his cabinet.
  • Rates split: Russia cut to 14% while forecasting 0-1% growth, the Fed is set to hold a fifth time, and analysts warn oil, tariffs and AI spending could revive inflation.
